lesson.title: Notes to Your Future Self: Writing Comments
lesson.summary: A comment is text in a source file that the Python interpreter completely ignores, written purely to help a human reader understand what the code is doing and why.
lesson.body:
Code tells a computer exactly what to do, but it does not always explain why that particular approach was chosen, and that missing context can be just as important as the instructions themselves. Comments exist to fill that gap. In Python, any text on a line after a hash symbol, #, is a comment, and the interpreter skips over it entirely when running the script, treating it as if it were not there at all. A comment can take up an entire line by itself, or it can follow a line of real code, in which case everything from the hash symbol to the end of that line is ignored while the code before it still runs normally.

Return to the script from the previous chapter, now with comments added:

# Convert Celsius to Fahrenheit using the standard formula
celsius = 20
fahrenheit = celsius * 9 / 5 + 32  # true division keeps the decimal
print(fahrenheit)

Tracing this file, the interpreter skips the first line entirely, since it begins with #. On the third line, it executes celsius * 9 / 5 + 32 exactly as before, ignoring everything from the # true division keeps the decimal portion onward, because that text comes after the code on the line, not before it. The output is identical to the version without comments: 68.0. This is the key property of comments to internalize, they never change what a program does, they only add information for a person reading the source file later.

Good comments explain why a piece of code exists or why one approach was chosen over another, not simply what the code already says plainly. A comment like # add 1 to x placed above a line that reads x = x + 1 adds nothing, since anyone who can read Python already knows that line adds 1 to x. A more useful comment might explain a non-obvious reason, such as noting that a formula follows a specific standard or that a value was hardcoded because of a known limitation elsewhere in the system. Comments can also be used to temporarily disable a line of code during debugging, a practice often called commenting out, by placing a # in front of a line so the interpreter skips it without deleting it, which is convenient for testing a program with and without a particular step.

One risk worth knowing about is that comments can become misleading if the code around them changes but the comment is never updated, leaving a note that no longer describes what the code actually does. Because of this, experienced programmers try to keep comments accurate over time and prefer writing clear, self-explanatory code over relying on comments to explain confusing code. A stale comment that contradicts the code beneath it is often worse than no comment at all, since a reader may trust the comment and misunderstand what the program actually does.

Comments are legal anywhere in a Python file, including inside a REPL session, though they are far more valuable in saved scripts, since that is where future readers, including your own future self, will actually rely on them. As scripts grow longer than the tiny examples used so far, often spanning many functions written by more than one person over time, a short comment explaining an unusual decision can save a future reader a great deal of time compared to having to work out the reasoning from the code alone.
